analysis.one_liner: Forces cable, internet, and phone companies to advertise the real all-in price and bans forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, after all 14 of its Senate supporters were Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required internet, cable TV, and phone companies to advertise only the full price a customer would actually pay, including equipment rental and administrative fees. It would have required itemized electronic bills, 21 days' notice plus a penalty-free exit whenever a company raised charges mid-contract, a ban on raising equipment rental fees without a real upgrade, and a prohibition on contract clauses forcing customers into arbitration instead of court. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and small businesses that pay for internet, cable TV, and phone service. They would see the true total price upfront instead of a low advertised rate padded with junk fees, get itemized bills, be able to cancel without penalty when fees go up, and keep the right to sue in court over billing disputes.

how_it_helps.text: Providers could not advertise a price unless it was the total amount the customer would actually be charged, including taxes the provider itself controls, administrative fees, and equipment rental fees; only government-mandated taxes that vary by locality could stay out of the advertised price [S3].

Electronic bills could only be sent if the customer was notified by email and the bill broke out the service charge, taxes, administrative fees, and equipment rental line by line, at the detail of a paper bill [S3].
Any increase in charges, however small, required clear notice at least 21 days beforehand and the right to end the contract without an early-termination fee or penalty [S3].
Providers could not raise equipment rental fees unless the equipment received a hardware or software upgrade with a substantial increase in functionality [S3].
Contracts could not require customers to settle billing disputes through alternative dispute resolution; any such clause would be void and unenforceable [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Internet, cable, and phone providers. Advertising all-in prices, itemizing bills, and forfeiting fee-notice games would compress the revenue they collect from hidden and recurring fees, and dropping forced arbitration would expose them to billing lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The advertising rule had a carve-out: government-mandated taxes that are not uniform nationwide did not have to be included in the advertised price, so the advertised figure could still fall short of the final bill in areas with heavy local utility taxes [S3].

The bill relied on the Federal Communications Commission to police functional equivalents of email and services 'used to evade' the rules, and it carried no new enforcement funding or private right of action beyond voiding arbitration clauses, so compliance would depend on agency attention [S3].

Providers argued in general that all-in pricing can raise the sticker price customers see at a glance even when it is more honest, and that ending forced arbitration adds litigation costs that can be passed through; neither claim nor industry response appears in the congressional record for this bill [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are straightforward and low-cost for households: honest advertised prices, itemized bills, and an exit ramp when fees rise. The main real trade-offs are the advertising carve-out for local taxes and the cost to companies of abandoning fee revenue and forced arbitration. The bill was narrow and never debated, so no committee-amended version existed to weigh.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the bill on February 14, 2019, joined by six original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
Thirteen senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action was recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote, and the bill died with the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet, cable, and phone companies kept the status quo: low advertised prices padded with equipment and administrative fees, automatic mid-contract fee increases, and arbitration clauses blocking billing lawsuits. Customers kept paying the junk fees the bill targeted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cable and phone companies kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the TRUE Fees Act on February 14, 2019, and took no further recorded action on it after it was referred to committee.

for.name: 13 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Blumenthal, Klobuchar, Cardin, Warren, Wyden, and Smith.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 14, 2019 and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor, so no vote ever occurred; no Republican senator cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 supporters — the sponsor plus 13 cosponsors — were Democrats, no Republican signed on, and the bill died without a vote in a Senate run by Republicans.

industries.note: These companies advertise teaser rates and collect billions through equipment rental and 'administrative' fees that appear later in the bill. The bill would force the all-in price into the ad, cap equipment fee hikes at genuine upgrades, and let customers exit without penalty when charges rise — directly cutting into that fee revenue.

industries.industry: Forced arbitration and alternative dispute resolution industry
industries.note: Consumer contracts from these providers routinely require arbitration for billing disputes, sending cases to private arbiters instead of court. Banning such clauses would remove a stream of cases and let customers sue in court.

industries.industry: Telecom and cable advertising and marketing
industries.note: Promotional pricing built on a low headline number and small-print fees is a core marketing tool in this sector. All-in price advertising would force a rewrite of those offers.
